presentingComplaint: Painful mouth ulcers, red eyes, and a spreading rash with skin peeling for 3 days, starting 8 days after being started on lamotrigine for a mood disorder.
history: 34-year-old woman started on lamotrigine 12 days ago (with rapid dose escalation outside recommended titration) for bipolar disorder. Five days later she developed fever, sore throat, and malaise, initially attributed to a viral illness. Two days after that she noticed burning painful erosions in her mouth and conjunctival redness/grittiness, followed within 24 hours by a tender, dusky-red macular rash starting on the trunk and face and spreading to the limbs. Over the next 2 days the skin began to blister and slough off with gentle pressure. She reports odynophagia limiting oral intake, photophobia, and pain on urination. No other new drugs, supplements, or recent infections. No prior history of similar reaction. No known drug allergies previously documented.
examination: Acutely unwell, febrile, and in visible pain. Widespread dusky erythematous and purpuric macules coalescing into sheets over face, trunk, and proximal limbs (~15% body surface area with epidermal detachment), with positive Nikolsky sign at the margins of blisters. Hemorrhagic crusting of the lips and buccal mucosa, oral erosions, bilateral conjunctival injection with mucopurulent discharge, and erosions of the labia minora. No epidermal detachment involving palms/soles. No lymphadenopathy. Chest and abdomen otherwise unremarkable; no hepatosplenomegaly.
imaging: Chest X-ray: no consolidation or effusion (baseline prior to potential respiratory mucosal involvement)
microbiology: Blood cultures pending, drawn to exclude concurrent sepsis given fever and tachycardia
Skin swab/biopsy sent for histopathology (full-thickness epidermal necrosis with subepidermal split expected) and to exclude staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome and infective causes

finalDiagnosis: Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis overlap (SJS/TEN), drug-induced (lamotrigine), mucocutaneous variant with ~15% BSA epidermal detachment

contraindications: Lamotrigine and all structurally related/cross-reactive drugs must be permanently discontinued and documented as an absolute allergy
Avoid empirical prophylactic systemic antibiotics unless culture-confirmed secondary infection is documented (risk of further drug reaction and resistance)
Avoid sulfonamides, allopurinol, and other high-risk SJS/TEN-associated drugs given demonstrated hypersensitivity predisposition
Avoid adhesive dressings and unnecessary skin trauma given Nikolsky-positive skin
Systemic corticosteroids/IVIG use is controversial and should follow specialist (burns/dermatology) unit protocols, not routine primary-care management
edgeCases: If body surface area of detachment exceeds 30%, this reclassifies as toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) rather than SJS, changing prognosis and mandating burns-unit-level care
Concurrent fever and tachycardia raise concern for evolving sepsis/toxic shock or secondary skin infection, which must be actively excluded rather than assumed to be part of the primary drug reaction
Rapid lamotrigine dose escalation and concomitant valproate use (not present here) are well-recognized risk factors that should be specifically asked about
Ocular involvement requires urgent ophthalmology co-management to prevent symblepharon and long-term visual sequelae
